claims.text: Boride-coated components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment suffer aggressive attack by molten aluminum.
An ultrathin alumina coating several nanometers thick can be deposited on the boride-based component by ALD.
The ALD-deposited alumina layer will be dense.
Adding an ultrathin alumina surface layer will improve the corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
The alumina layer will act as an effective diffusion barrier during molten-aluminum exposure.
Temperatures of 600–750 °C are typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating.
The deposited alumina layer will be chemically inert and adherent under the proposed exposure conditions.
The alumina layer will suppress aluminum diffusion into or through the underlying boride layer.
The alumina layer will suppress interfacial reactions between molten aluminum and the boride layer.
Alumina is thermodynamically stable under the stated molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
By providing a physical and chemical barrier, alumina will reduce interdiffusion and chemical attack at the boride–aluminum interface.
ALD-alumina-coated components will exhibit lower weight loss than untreated boride-coated controls after prolonged molten-aluminum exposure.
ALD-alumina-coated components will retain a more intact surface microstructure than untreated boride-coated controls.
The protective effect is expected to persist during continuous molten-aluminum contact at 600–750 °C.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement will depend on alumina-layer thickness, coating quality, and long-term adhesion under thermal cycling.
